source: Leonxlnx/cinetic techniques.json (MIT), trimmed to tool-agnostic fields

techniques.name: Four live cells from frame 2
techniques.summary: There is no title. The film opens on a flush 2x2 grid where every cell is already mid-action (a line assembling, a counter ticking, an object orbiting, a pin dropping), so from its first frames the frame reads as one living system.
techniques.use_when: A hero or social loop that must show several features at once, or a launch whose first second has to prove breadth.
techniques.avoid_when: The story needs one idea at a time, a single-message sting, or a 9:16 frame where the cells would shrink below about 540 px wide.

techniques.name: Macro number scramble, one-frame snap-out
techniques.summary: Huge digits fill and overflow the frame, re-rolling every frame. On one frame the view cuts back to the whole figure, which rolls into the final metric and holds: the number is the hook before any brand appears.
techniques.use_when: The strongest proof is one metric (users, hours saved, uptime) and the film earns attention with the outcome before the brand.
techniques.avoid_when: There is no credible or impressive number, or the tone is calm and premium.

techniques.name: Mark builds, then is thrown into a macro of itself
techniques.summary: On frame 1 a dot swells into the brand mark. The mark grows briefly, holds for a breath, then shrinks away faster and faster and hard-cuts at peak speed to a frame-filling macro of the same mark, which keeps pulling back.
techniques.use_when: A brand-first logo sting where recognition must land in under half a second and the energy must pour into the next shot.
techniques.avoid_when: The mark is unfamiliar and needs a longer hold to be learned, or the film already uses a scale-continuity cut elsewhere. Never use it to show the full lockup.

techniques.name: Sparse intro, drop on the first hard cut
techniques.summary: (Sound and picture.) The first ~2 s carry only light plucks or a filtered, wide pad under the opening type; the low end and the kick land exactly on the frame where the punchline card or first product shot cuts in.
techniques.use_when: Almost any film that opens on type and then shows the product with a tension-and-release shape.
techniques.avoid_when: Stings under 4 s, openers designed to be loud from frame 0 (live grid, macro scramble), or a drop that cannot land on a whole-frame cut.

techniques.name: Cursor into a field, two-stage push, typed provocation
techniques.summary: A small search pill sits still on a dark stage; a text cursor drifts in, the camera pushes in twice to a macro framing, and a provocative query types into the field before any brand appears.
techniques.use_when: AI, search or command products, or any opener whose hook is a question the product answers.
techniques.avoid_when: The product has no input field, the film's camera grammar is flat, or the query runs past about 40 characters (the macro framing cannot hold it).

techniques.name: Oversize line flies through, restarts small
techniques.summary: A huge fragment of the headline, about a quarter of frame height, brakes in from the right with its letters fading on as it slows, then dissolves; three frames later the same line restarts small and centred so it can be read.
techniques.use_when: The headline has a thesis word worth previewing big, in a dark, energetic launch.
techniques.avoid_when: Light stages where 65% white loses contrast, or headlines longer than about 5 words whose big fragment will not read. Also avoid it when the big fragment would sit still and cropped at both edges at any point: viewers read an oversized, cropped line that vanishes and then restarts small as a false start, not a preview. It has to travel every frame it is on screen.

techniques.name: Problem pile-up, freeze, turn
techniques.summary: The film opens inside the problem: cards, alerts or rows pile in faster and faster while a counter climbs, the picture freezes for a breath of true silence, and the turn hits on the downbeat.
techniques.use_when: Problem-first launches whose pain is volume: notifications, tickets, tabs, invoices.
techniques.avoid_when: The pain is not about quantity, the brand film is calm, or the film already uses its one freeze elsewhere.

techniques.name: Finished result first, then rewind
techniques.summary: The film opens on the finished end state at its most impressive, holds for a beat, then visibly rewinds every element back to the empty start, where the story begins playing forward.
techniques.use_when: Walkthroughs and feature films whose output is visually rich and readable at a glance.
techniques.avoid_when: An end state that needs explaining, or more than about 30 state changes (the rewind turns to mush).

techniques.name: A click starts the film
techniques.summary: From frame 0 a cursor is already travelling toward the one button on an otherwise bare stage; it presses, and the button floods open into the first scene.
techniques.use_when: UI walkthroughs and feature films where a single action is the product ('one click to ...').
techniques.avoid_when: Products that act on their own, or films where the cursor never returns after the hook (it breaks continuity).

techniques.name: Cut in mid-sentence, pull back to the line
techniques.summary: The film opens inside one giant word, its first letter cropped by the frame edge as if cutting into a thought mid-sentence; after a beat the camera pulls back to reveal the whole sentence at reading size.
techniques.use_when: Copy-led launches built on one charged word, in calm-to-medium films.
techniques.avoid_when: The key word is short or ordinary (the crop will not intrigue), or the film already opens on another zoom-out (icon card, macro number).

techniques.name: Velocity handoff cut
techniques.summary: The outgoing shot speeds up in one direction and is cut on its fastest frame. The next shot opens already moving the same way and brakes to rest, so momentum runs straight through the edit.
techniques.use_when: Most cuts between moving shots: feature-to-feature edits, montages, chapter changes, and any film that must never stop. Velocity-matched cuts are exempt from the two-uses-per-type limit.
techniques.avoid_when: One side has to be still (a held statement or a designed freeze), or the two shots would move in opposite directions. Carry a shape or an anchor across instead.

techniques.name: Scale-through cut
techniques.summary: An object shrinks faster and faster toward a fixed point, the film cuts, and a matching object appears much larger on the same point and keeps shrinking as it brakes, so one pull-back runs through two different worlds. The mirror version swells into the cut and opens on an undersized object that grows.
techniques.use_when: Changing medium or world while keeping the subject: 3D to flat, device to UI, brand card to product, a mark coming back as a macro. Also hero pull-backs at act changes.
techniques.avoid_when: The two objects cannot share a centre point, or both sides are calm; a scale jump without matched scale velocity reads as a jump cut. Use it at most twice per film.

techniques.name: Anchored overlay, background swap
techniques.summary: A foreground element (a pin, a status pill, a modal, a big word) keeps its exact screen position while the world behind it hard-cuts, so a total change of scene reads as a change of zoom or context.
techniques.use_when: Showing that one thing persists across contexts: a location going from 3D city to map, a request going from an empty void to the full app, a claim held over a run of photos.
techniques.avoid_when: The overlay is text that must be reread after each swap, or the backgrounds are busy and bright enough to swallow it. Keep backgrounds near 5% mean luma under light overlays.

techniques.name: Polarity flip cut
techniques.summary: A hard cut flips the stage between near-black and near-white on a downbeat, often with the same icon or pill held on the same spot in inverted colours, so the luminance jump itself is the accent.
techniques.use_when: Act breaks: problem to answer, public to private, demo to claim. The strongest punctuation on a drop.
techniques.avoid_when: A third time in one film; a flip from a static frame with nothing carried; or when the accent field would be the film's second full-frame accent flood.

techniques.name: Shape match cut
techniques.summary: The hero shape leaves one shot at a known point and size, and the next shot opens on a matching shape (the mark, the flat UI, the real object) on the same point, so the object's identity carries across a change of world.
techniques.use_when: Turning a problem shape into the answer, a device mockup into the bare UI, or a physical object into the mark.
techniques.avoid_when: The silhouettes differ (round against tall), so the match cannot be seen. Use a dot relay or a container morph instead.

techniques.name: Giant word punch-out
techniques.summary: A hard cut lands on an extreme close-up of an oversized word sliding fast and braking, its letters resolving one by one. A second cut jumps out to the whole word at reading size, arriving with wide tracking that slams together.
techniques.use_when: A one-word claim or product name that deserves two beats: read it, then see it whole. Vertical cut-downs where one huge word fills the frame.
techniques.avoid_when: Lines of more than two words, or words over about 10 letters (the close-up loses the word); or when the next shot needs the word small within a second.

techniques.name: Collapse to a dot relay
techniques.summary: The hero collapses into one small dot, or the whole world shrinks into it. The dot, the only thing that survives, opens into the next object: a check ring, an avatar, the mark.
techniques.use_when: Submit, send, process, receive: actions that mean 'this went in and came out as that'. Also the film's signature device when the mark contains a dot.
techniques.avoid_when: The dot would blink out or change size or colour at the seam, or the film already has an implosion seam.

techniques.name: Defocus cut
techniques.summary: The outgoing shot throws itself out of focus in a few frames, the film cuts to a shot that is still fully defocused with its content already moving, and the lens snaps sharp as that content settles.
techniques.use_when: Joining two shots with nothing in common (no shared shape, direction or colour), or a deliberate 'look again' beat.
techniques.avoid_when: As the default seam (it turns into a soft crossfade), on shots dominated by small text, or more than twice per film.

techniques.name: Path relay
techniques.summary: A line and its lead dot carry the eye from one place to the next. The connector bends around a rounded corner with the camera following, or continues across a cut and enters the next shot from the same edge at the same angle.
techniques.use_when: Money, data or messages travelling (send, route, sync), flowcharts and timelines, and films whose UI already uses lines and nodes.
techniques.avoid_when: The film has no line language, or the path would cross readable text. A path that loops back reads as indecision.

techniques.name: Iris from a glyph
techniques.summary: A small dot appears on a word or icon in the current shot and balloons exponentially to swallow the frame, showing the next scene inside it, so the reveal starts from content rather than from nowhere.
techniques.use_when: A word in the copy names what the next scene shows (a benchmark, a feature, a place); dark-to-light or light-to-dark act changes.
techniques.avoid_when: A linear radius (it crawls, then snaps); the same iris more than twice per film; a seed glyph the viewer has not had 6 f to find.

techniques.name: Portal zoom with aspect morph
techniques.summary: A window opens in the middle of a solid tile. Tile and window grow faster and faster while the square stretches to 16:9, until the window's interior is the next scene and the tile's border has flown off the edges.
techniques.use_when: The film's energy peak and act break, going inside the product, when the mark or app icon is a tile.
techniques.avoid_when: The accent has already flooded the frame once (the tile border is a brief accent flood), or another zoom-through sits in the same act.

techniques.name: Band wipe
techniques.summary: A band crosses a region (snapping up, lingering, then whipping off, or sweeping across a chart) and the content changes along its edge: the old state is erased under it and the new state draws in its wake.
techniques.use_when: Swapping a data series, a filter result or a big-type card in place, when a control's tap should visibly cause the change.
techniques.avoid_when: Applied to whole scenes again and again (it becomes a preset wipe), or when the band would cross text the viewer has not finished reading.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Fill the band with the one accent (or ink on a paper stage) at full strength. Its trailing side falls off by opacity of that same colour over 30-40% of its width, with no light core, no screen blend and no second hue.

techniques.name: Horizon rise
techniques.summary: A huge disc rises from the bottom edge like a planet horizon, its rim washing over the frame, until its dark core swallows the screen and becomes the stage for the next line.
techniques.use_when: A single colour event that divides the film into acts (UI section to brand moment), or a calm lift from a statement into the next card.
techniques.avoid_when: More than once per film, or on a light film where the dark core would be the only dark frame.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Keep one hue: the dark core, then a rim of the accent at full strength falling off by opacity of that same accent (no second hue, no bloom), baked dithered. Or use a hard-edged ink disc with a 1.5 px accent edge rising over a paper stage.

techniques.name: Product surface cover wipe
techniques.summary: A product surface (a UI panel, a window, a device) moves in front of the old shot and either passes straight through it with the scene changed behind it, or lands and becomes the new shot.
techniques.use_when: Promise to product: the UI pushes the headline off. Scene changes that should show the product itself rather than a graphic.
techniques.avoid_when: The surface is a plain coloured slab (then it is a preset wipe), or the pass-through would need more than 80 px/f; shorten the distance with a cut instead.

techniques.name: Reveal by subtraction
techniques.summary: The clutter in front of the hero flies off toward the frame edges or shrinks away, uncovering a hero that was already sitting at its final size behind it.
techniques.use_when: Ending a busy montage on the one stat, card or word. Walkthroughs that change app areas through the product's own window behaviour.
techniques.avoid_when: The hero is not ready behind the clutter (it must never pop in), or the clutter is readable content the viewer has not finished.

techniques.name: Conveyor line swap
techniques.summary: The current line floats up and fades, the stage is empty for an instant, and the next line rises from below into the same spot, so a run of statements reads as one upward feed.
techniques.use_when: Sequences of short claims, lists of capabilities, a subject that changes while the predicate stays.
techniques.avoid_when: Lines of very different length or alignment (the eye loses the slot), or more than 4-5 lines in a row without another seam type.

techniques.name: Motion-masked swap
techniques.summary: Content changes on exactly the frame something else moves fastest (background rings whipping past, a card kicking into a tilt), so the change hides inside the motion and two states chain in one space with no visible cut.
techniques.use_when: Changing copy inside a continuous environment; cycling examples (photos, prompts, results) in a loop.
techniques.avoid_when: The masking motion is weak (under about 20 px/f at its peak), so the swap shows; or the content is a counter (roll the digits instead).

techniques.name: Tip-back exit
techniques.summary: The outgoing scene tips away from camera like a sheet laid onto a table, or flips up into a line, speeding up and fading into the next stage colour, and the next element lands on the clean field.
techniques.use_when: Ending a UI section to hand over to a statement or an alert, when the next beat needs an empty stage for big type.
techniques.avoid_when: The next act opens on the same pose (use a relay instead), or the dim would go to black and back up (a dip) instead of into the next stage colour.

techniques.name: Envelope-matched type cut
techniques.summary: A big line hard-cuts to a much smaller, longer line whose words start spread apart so it spans exactly the old line's width, then the gaps close while the sideways drift carries on, so the outer edges of the type survive the cut.
techniques.use_when: A big two- or three-word claim hands over to its full sentence or call to action; any big-to-small type change where both lines share a centre or a left edge and the type already drifts sideways.
techniques.avoid_when: B is naturally wider than A (use a blur-swap rescale instead), either line is a single word (there are no gaps, so collapse one word's tracking instead), or the alignment changes across the cut.

techniques.name: Angle change on a shared drift
techniques.summary: A hard cut jumps to a new angle or the next state of the same object (front to top-down, open to closed) while the slow zoom or pan carries on at exactly the same rate, so a calm shot changes viewpoint with no jolt and no speed ramp.
techniques.use_when: Calm films and product beauty shots where a velocity ramp would be too loud: showing an object's second side or its next state within one continuous gesture.
techniques.avoid_when: The two angles look alike (under about 30 deg it reads as a jump cut), the subject's size or position jumps, or one side is static. For a lift in energy, use a velocity handoff instead.

techniques.name: Select and retype swap
techniques.summary: A finished headline is selected like text in an editor, the highlight holds for a beat, and on one frame the selection is replaced by a caret that types the next line in the same place.
techniques.use_when: Products where text is the medium (editors, prompts, writing and AI tools); correcting a claim, where the assumption is selected and overwritten by the answer; two or three headline swaps that should feel authored.
techniques.avoid_when: The product has nothing to do with text, lines run past about 40 characters (the typing outlasts the read), or the swap repeats more than three times in a row and turns into a typing demo.

techniques.name: Stepped column fill
techniques.summary: Columns rise from the bottom edge in a stepped pyramid centred under the hero, spreading outward until they close into one solid field that becomes the next stage behind it.
techniques.use_when: Marks built from bars, steps or pixels; data and analytics products, where the columns read as a chart; stings and loop intros that change the stage colour behind a held hero.
techniques.avoid_when: As a general scene change between unrelated shots (it reads as a preset blinds wipe), behind small readable type, or more than once per film.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Fill every column with one flat colour: the next stage colour, or the accent if this is the film's one accent flood. Or alternate two adjacent lightness steps of one hue from column to column and let them merge into a single tone as the field closes. Never put a ramp inside a column.

techniques.name: Living hold creep
techniques.summary: Under every hold the frame keeps a barely visible push, pull or sideways drift, so no shot sits dead while the viewer reads.
techniques.use_when: Any hold longer than about 30 f: reading a caption, watching a counter, a UI state sitting after an action, the end card.
techniques.avoid_when: A designed freeze of at most 15 f on a silence, or a shot where a big camera move or a travelling cursor already supplies the life. Never stack a creep on top of a punch-in drift on the same axis.

techniques.name: Breathing zoom between interactions
techniques.summary: After a reveal the camera slowly pulls back, coasts through a stop and turns smoothly into a slow push that lands on the next interaction, so the frame breathes across a whole act.
techniques.use_when: Dashboard, analytics or table acts of 4-10 s with several interactions in one framing, where cutting would cost orientation.
techniques.avoid_when: Shots shorter than about 90 f, acts that already move pose to pose with big pushes, or a scrolling feed (a zoom on a moving list reads as wobble).

techniques.name: Punch-in insert on the same render
techniques.summary: A hard cut jumps from the wide view to a 2-2.5x on-axis close-up, or to a 3-4.5x macro of the exact control being used, while every animation keeps running, then cuts back out.
techniques.use_when: Small UI actions that need hero weight (send, picking a date, a chip), long walkthroughs that need their visual scale reset, and a wide/close rhythm that keeps both context and legibility.
techniques.avoid_when: The UI doesn't hold up at 3-4.5x, or the close-up isn't obviously the same place (keep the cut on-axis or anchored to the cursor, or it reads as a jump).

techniques.name: Detail first, then pull back
techniques.summary: A shot opens tight on the one thing that matters (giant prompt words, a chart counting up, a status pill) with no chrome, then the camera pulls back to show it sitting in the full window.
techniques.use_when: Result reveals, analytics, prompts and input moments where the value should land before the load of the full UI; breaking up a repeated card formula; re-establishing the whole product after a run of close details.
techniques.avoid_when: The product hasn't been seen yet and the tight frame stays unrecognisable for long (keep the tight hold under 52 f), or the wider frame adds nothing new.

techniques.name: Hero push with a 3D turn
techniques.summary: From a wide view of the whole app, one continuous move pushes 2.5x into a single panel while yawing, so the panel turns toward the viewer and an empty side of the frame opens for the caption.
techniques.use_when: The film's energy peak: the one feature that needs both spatial orientation and close-up legibility, or a scene change inside a single-take film.
techniques.avoid_when: More than once per film, or on a lone card with no surrounding app (the turn needs a world to orient against). Keep each act on its own rotation axis.

techniques.name: Dolly surge with a foreground pass
techniques.summary: The camera surges from a wide shot into a 3x medium close-up, with most of the travel in half a second, and at the fastest moment a near object rushes past the lens before a long, slow creep.
techniques.use_when: Opening a launch film into a 3D or layered world, or a sting that dives from an overview into the hero object.
techniques.avoid_when: Flat UI with no depth layers (nothing to pass the lens), or calm walkthroughs.

techniques.name: Push-in with a roll swing
techniques.summary: The camera dives into one corner of the UI, rolls a few degrees off level mid-dive like a hand-steered move, and rolls back to level as it lands.
techniques.use_when: A push that would otherwise feel mechanical: diving into a settings corner, a sidebar or a detail panel.
techniques.avoid_when: Next to another rolled or tilted move in the same act (one rotation axis per act), or on moves shorter than 40 f, where the roll reads as a wobble.

techniques.name: Isolating push into one item
techniques.summary: The camera pushes into one row, card or column while everything around it fades, dims or slides off the edges, picking a single thread out of a busy layout.
techniques.use_when: Choosing one result from a list of parallel processes, moving from a typographic act into a UI close-up without a cut, or steering the eye to where the next action will happen.
techniques.avoid_when: The item is still too small to read at 4x, or the surrounding layout carries information the viewer still needs.

techniques.name: Reactive reframe
techniques.summary: When something new appears (a popover, a result, the hero icon), the camera glides a few hundred pixels and pushes in slightly until it sits where the eye wants it.
techniques.use_when: After any UI event that changes what matters on screen, or after a punch-in that left the hero off-centre.
techniques.avoid_when: Every small UI change (keep it for the ones that matter), or an element that already appears near frame centre (a move under 40 px reads as a twitch).

techniques.name: Pull-back that lands an event
techniques.summary: A long, gentle pull-back runs from a close-up to the full view, and as it decelerates the next UI event (a modal, labels, a caption) starts, so it lands together with the camera's settle.
techniques.use_when: Walkthroughs and single-take films that move pose to pose, and any long move whose ending would otherwise be a dead beat.
techniques.avoid_when: Short or fast moves under 50 f, where an event in the tail just competes with the motion, and the finale, where the lockup needs a clean frame.

techniques.name: Cursor-led whip orbit
techniques.summary: Following a cursor that leads the way to the next panel, the camera swings fast across the product, yawing to show the slab's thick edge and rolling slightly.
techniques.use_when: Moving between two distant panels of one product in a single-take or walkthrough film, where a cut would lose the spatial relationship.
techniques.avoid_when: There is no cursor or other lead to motivate it (an unmotivated whip reads as a flourish), or the act already uses yaw for something else.

techniques.name: Off-frame whip relay
techniques.summary: The cursor accelerates up and out of frame, the camera whips down the product while it's hidden, and the cursor re-enters from the top as a fast streak that brakes onto its target.
techniques.use_when: A big spatial jump within one product (top bar to bottom bar, one page to another) that should feel like a match-on-action without a cut.
techniques.avoid_when: Films without a cursor, or destinations less than about one frame height away (a plain reframe is enough).

techniques.name: Follow the lead dot
techniques.summary: A small lead (a progress dot, a travelling packet, a drawing line's head) moves through the layout and the camera follows it with a soft lag, never quite stopping, so the viewer always knows where to look.
techniques.use_when: Agent progress, pipelines, timelines and journeys across a map: any story told by one thing moving through a layout.
techniques.avoid_when: The lead moves faster than about 20 px/f for long stretches (the lag lets it escape the frame), or the whole layout fits in one framing.

techniques.name: Crane down with a delayed push
techniques.summary: The camera tilts down the page past the chart to the detail cards while a slow push-in builds behind it, as if the operator were leaning in to read.
techniques.use_when: Moving down a long page or dashboard from the overview to the detail that matters.
techniques.avoid_when: Pages too short to travel 500 px or more, or vertical formats where the push crops the column.

techniques.name: Extrude then crash in
techniques.summary: An object grows toward camera (a disc extruding into a tall cylinder) and the camera slams into it, hard-cutting to its interior while still rushing forward.
techniques.use_when: A violent spatial jump into the product at the energy peak of a launch film or sting.
techniques.avoid_when: Calm films, any second use in the same film, and readable text on either side of the cut.

techniques.name: Directional impact kick
techniques.summary: On a true impact (a card landing, a lock-in, a slam) the whole frame jolts a few pixels in the direction of the hit and pushes a hair closer, then settles within a fifth of a second.
techniques.use_when: True landings and lock-ins: a heavy object slamming into a slot, or a statement locking together on a hit.
techniques.avoid_when: Every beat or tick (that makes a shake, not a hit), soft UI arrivals, or mid camera move (it fights the move's ease).

techniques.name: Layered parallax truck
techniques.summary: The camera trucks sideways across a scene split into two or three depth planes: the background barely moves, the subject moves with the camera and a near element slides past faster, so a flat layout reads as space.
techniques.use_when: Hero product shots and feature cards that need depth without 3D, and slow establishing moves.
techniques.avoid_when: Dense UI walkthroughs where the eye has to track one control, or any scene with more than three planes (it starts to look like a parallax demo).

techniques.name: Seamless loop drift
techniques.summary: In a looping clip the camera drifts along a slow, closed figure-eight (a little sideways, a little up, breathing in and out) and returns exactly to its first frame, so the loop has no seam.
techniques.use_when: Feature loops, background clips and vertical loops that replay endlessly.
techniques.avoid_when: Linear films with cuts (use a living hold instead), or loops shorter than about 4 s, where the drift turns into a visible wobble.

techniques.name: Pull out from inside the object
techniques.summary: The shot opens on what reads as a full-bleed colour field or a statement card, and one long pull reveals it was the face of a small object (an app icon, a card, a screen, the mark) sitting among its neighbours.
techniques.use_when: Cold opens and hooks where a calm statement or a colour field should turn out to be part of the product (the question was printed on the app icon, the colour was one card in the grid); landing the mark into the final lockup; any reveal whose point is scale.
techniques.avoid_when: The face is a photo or bitmap (it falls apart at 8-14x), the context it lands in is not recognisable at a glance, or a scale-through cut or detail-first pull-back has already used the same object. Once per film.

techniques.name: Fly-through of a depth field
techniques.summary: Dozens of flat screens or tokens float at different depths and the camera travels forward through them: near ones swell and slide off the frame edges, far ones barely drift, until the move lands square on one hero screen.
techniques.use_when: Proving breadth (a whole platform, hundreds of templates, every integration) in 3-4 s without explaining any single screen; opening into a layered world; arriving on the one screen the next act is about.
techniques.avoid_when: Items must be read in flight, there are fewer than about 15 of them (the field looks sparse), the film is flat with no depth language, or lc-swarm-cluster-burst already spends the film's breadth crescendo.

techniques.name: Fit-to-content follow
techniques.summary: As a route, graph or plan builds, the camera widens just enough to keep every piece that matters in frame, so the shot opens close on the first node and ends on the whole structure.
techniques.use_when: Pipelines, agent plans, org charts, dependency or network graphs and routes that build piece by piece, where the first node needs close-up legibility and the payoff is the whole shape.
techniques.avoid_when: The finished structure already fits one comfortable framing, a single moving lead is the whole story (cam-lead-follow), or the full structure cannot fit with 24 px labels (split it into chapters with cuts instead).

techniques.name: Zoom-out hop between areas
techniques.summary: To travel between two distant parts of one product, the camera eases back as it sets off, crosses at a wider framing that shows where it is going, and pushes back in as it arrives.
techniques.use_when: Single-take and walkthrough films moving between two areas of one surface more than about a frame width apart (sidebar to canvas, one dashboard panel to another), where the viewer should see how they relate.
techniques.avoid_when: Areas less than about a frame width apart (cam-reframe-to-subject), a cursor that should lead the move (cam-cursor-whip-orbit), or a wide view that is cluttered or unfinished, since the hop shows it.

techniques.name: Phrase clamp at a junction
techniques.summary: Two halves of a phrase arrive from opposite directions and lock on one baseline at a fixed junction, like a clamp closing.
techniques.use_when: A two-part claim whose halves mean more together (subject + promise, problem + fix); the payoff line; a junction that a slot roller will reuse.
techniques.avoid_when: Lines over 5 words or halves of very unequal length; more than once per film; the end lockup.

techniques.name: Slot roller beside a fixed phrase
techniques.summary: A fixed phrase holds still while the word in its slot rolls through alternatives one line at a time, speeding up until the last one lands.
techniques.use_when: One sentence frame that fits many subjects or capabilities; listing use-cases without spending screen time; a feature loop that cycles items.
techniques.avoid_when: Items of very different widths in a centred layout (the fixed phrase would have to move); more than about 7 items; any mask loose enough that the neighbours read as a list.

techniques.name: Masked baseline rise
techniques.summary: Each word rises out of an invisible line at its own baseline, tops of the glyphs first, as if cut out of the layout.
techniques.use_when: Editorial headlines and in-UI headings that must land fast (a 3-word line in under 0.5 s) without stealing focus; titles that build while the plane or camera is still moving.
techniques.avoid_when: Tight leading where the mask would clip the line above; a calm voice-paced read (use ty-blur-focus-word-rise); per-letter runs on anything but one short hero word.

techniques.name: Blur-to-focus word rise
techniques.summary: Words materialise one per beat out of a soft blur, rising a few pixels and darkening to full ink as they sharpen.
techniques.use_when: Calm, premium statements that keep pace with a voice-over or a slow bed; the opening line of a quiet film; light grounds.
techniques.avoid_when: High-energy acts or dense beats (the stagger is too slow); pale type on a pale ground (under 4.5:1); any blur left on readable text for more than 6 f.

techniques.name: In-place word light-up on beats
techniques.summary: The finished line is laid out from the start and its words light up in place, chunk by chunk on the beat, with the last word held back.
techniques.use_when: Titles and walkthrough captions over a moving camera; lines with an inline glyph or partner wordmark that must not shift; music-led films where each chunk can sit on a beat.
techniques.avoid_when: High-energy acts that need motion in the type itself; lines over 6 words (it turns into a slide).

techniques.name: Time-boxed eased type-on
techniques.summary: Text types in with most of the line appearing in the first few frames, and every line, short or long, finishes in the same musical length.
techniques.use_when: Prompts, search queries and names typed into the product; UI labels appearing while the camera trucks; keeping a run of typed beats on one musical length.
techniques.avoid_when: Statements nobody would type; keystroke clicks on every glyph (let the music carry it); letter-by-letter reveals of a name whose prefixes spell another word.

techniques.name: Re-centring line build
techniques.summary: Words or typed glyphs join a centred line one at a time while the whole line glides sideways so it is centred on every frame.
techniques.use_when: Speaking-pace builds, stat rows that widen as words arrive, centred typed headlines, any line whose final width is unknown while it builds.
techniques.avoid_when: Shifts over about 280 px per word (split the line instead); left-aligned layouts; a line that must keep an anchored element still (use ty-inplace-light-up-beats).

techniques.name: Staggered word roll
techniques.summary: The words of a phrase roll up and away one after another while their replacements rise in from below, so one sentence mutates instead of cutting.
techniques.use_when: Swapping one claim for the next in place; a URL replacing a tagline; a category word turning into the product name; a closing bookend that rolls the opening phrase into the brand line.
techniques.avoid_when: Swaps where nothing persists (a cut or ty-blur-swap-rescale reads cleaner); more than two rolls in a row without a different move between them.

techniques.name: Reading-order word exit
techniques.summary: Words leave one by one in reading order, each lifting a few pixels and vanishing, until only the hero element is left on screen.
techniques.use_when: Isolating a hero word or object before a match cut or zoom; clearing a statement gently before a calmer UI moment; mirroring a word-by-word entry.
techniques.avoid_when: Walkthrough captions just before a camera move: fade the whole caption at once over 26 f on E.smooth and finish 0-56 f before the move starts; exits that would hurry a payoff line.

techniques.name: One-word slam sequence
techniques.summary: A line is read one huge word at a time: each word hits oversized and blurred, settles, then is sucked away as the next word cuts in.
techniques.use_when: A punchy 3-5 word line on a strong beat; a problem statement or rhythmic claim; vertical formats where one word fills the screen.
techniques.avoid_when: More than one sequence per film; lines over 5 words; calm films; a card for a lone connector word (fold it into the next word).

techniques.name: Multi-direction slam assembly
techniques.summary: Each word of a short sentence flies in from a different side, oversized and streaked, and the sentence assembles on one baseline almost at once.
techniques.use_when: Re-spiking energy after a calm, read-paced card; a payoff line that needs a burst; 3-5 short words.
techniques.avoid_when: Long words that would cross each other in flight; straight after another high-energy type move; calm films.

techniques.name: Oversize word slide-in
techniques.summary: A huge word arrives streaked from beside the frame and brakes on a long tail, and a trailing word follows from further out and closes the gap so the phrase locks together.
techniques.use_when: The energy peak of a type act; a two-word claim; a cold open whose first frame already moves.
techniques.avoid_when: Long phrases; when screen direction must run the other way across the cut; small type.

techniques.name: Blur-swap rescale
techniques.summary: A big word blurs out and instantly re-forms smaller as the start of the full line, so the type changes scale without a rubbery size tween.
techniques.use_when: Going from one or two giant words to the full readable sentence; right after tr-giant-word-punch-out; any big-to-small type handoff inside one continuous take.
techniques.avoid_when: As a default between unrelated lines (it is not a crossfade substitute); small-to-small swaps; overlaps longer than 10 f, which read as a dissolve.

techniques.name: Hard-step edits that act out the copy
techniques.summary: The headline does what it says with one-frame edits: broken words click straight one at a time, or words delete from the end faster and faster.
techniques.use_when: Copy about fixing, undoing, cleaning up or simplifying; a deadpan joke beat; a problem line that should visibly go away.
techniques.avoid_when: Copy the motion would contradict; calm films; more than one per film.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Keep only the rotation-based broken states (letters fanned along an arc, or the word rotated -20 deg) and drop the skewX(15deg) state, which fakes an italic; the one-frame steps, the 2% punches and the accelerating deletes stay as they are.

techniques.name: Shared-letter morph
techniques.summary: One word turns into another: the letters both words share stay and slide into place while the new letters tumble in and click upright.
techniques.use_when: Two words that share letters and whose relationship is the point (before and after, problem and product); one memorable word turn per film.
techniques.avoid_when: Fewer than 2 shared letters; words longer than about 8 letters; fast films where 60 f of letter flight is too slow.

techniques.name: Scramble decode
techniques.summary: A string of random glyphs locks into the real text from left to right, or real letters roll through the alphabet into gibberish and back.
techniques.use_when: Keys, codes, private or encrypted values, numbers resolving, a short technical name in a feature beat.
techniques.avoid_when: Prose statements (it delays reading); the brand name in the end lockup; glints or sparkles on the glyphs.

techniques.name: Travelling front restyles a word
techniques.summary: A front sweeps left to right across a settled word and restyles each glyph as it passes, in colour or weight, sometimes with a cursor riding under it.
techniques.use_when: Turning a static big word into a moment of discovery; emphasising one or two promise words without a highlight shape; a change of voice mid-sentence.
techniques.avoid_when: Text still moving; sweeps whose half-restyled frames read as another word; colour and weight sweeps in the same film.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: A one-hue front (mute -> accent -> ink per glyph through mixColor) instead of a multi-hue band, and a variable-weight wave (400 -> 700) in the film's one sans instead of switching glyphs to a serif italic.

techniques.name: Words spill out from behind a mark
techniques.summary: A glyph or icon slides aside and the words shoot out from behind it, clipped at its edge, as if the mark were delivering the message.
techniques.use_when: An icon-led claim mid-film, or an opening line pushed out by the mark already in motion; a feature icon that introduces its own line; a mark or number that says the sentence.
techniques.avoid_when: The end lockup (it appears once and belongs to the end card); marks smaller than the cap height (nothing to hide behind); spills longer than about 360 px.

techniques.name: Vertical word stack
techniques.summary: In a tall frame each new word lands on its own line under the last while the stack rises one line, so the newest word always sits on the optical centre.
techniques.use_when: Vertical cut-downs where a horizontal line would be too small; speaking-pace statements on a phone-sized frame; one word per beat.
techniques.avoid_when: 16:9 masters (use ty-recentre-line-build); statements over 6 words; stacking two separate statements.

techniques.name: Slice-band glyph assembly
techniques.summary: Each letter builds up from thin horizontal slices that slide in from slightly different offsets at slightly different moments, faint and pale at first, until the word locks solid.
techniques.use_when: A product or feature name that should feel assembled or digital. A name set beside a modular or pixel mark, including the one end-lockup build when the film bookends with it. A short title after a quiet beat.
techniques.avoid_when: Lines over about 3 words, or type under 48 px (bands thinner than 3 px alias into noise). Prose. Delay spreads wide enough that the half-built word reads as broken for more than about 30 f. A film that already has a scramble decode.

techniques.name: Slice glitch into a speed streak
techniques.summary: A word jolts into sideways-displaced horizontal slices for two frames, then stretches into a solid capsule that races off as a streak, and the next word lands in its wake.
techniques.use_when: A speed or performance claim, where the word itself turns into motion. Handing a name off to a thread, packet or line that carries into the next scene. The 2 f slice alone on 'private', 'encrypted' or 'blocked'.
techniques.avoid_when: Calm films. More than once per film. Words wider than about 450 px at the smear, where the edge would pass 80 px/f. Long lines. Coloured fringes or a tint shift along the trail.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Make the streak a flat solid capsule in C.ink or C.white with a speed-scaled tail and true motion blur. No bloom on the type or the streak, the trail keeps the capsule's one tone, and the glitch copies stay in C.mute.

techniques.name: Scaled-echo extrusion
techniques.summary: A hero title carries two or three faint copies scaled out behind it, a short depth extrusion that compresses as the title lands and then holds.
techniques.use_when: A product name or a hero title of one to three words that needs weight in a flat sans. A giant cropped word that needs physical depth. A title card between two energetic acts.
techniques.avoid_when: Body copy or lines over 3 words (the copies tangle inside the counters). Low-contrast stages, where the copies turn to haze. Blur, glow, bevels or drop shadows on the copies. A film that already uses the motion-trail echo of the word slams: pick one echo device.

techniques.name: Quiet type swells on the drop
techniques.summary: A word appears small and low-contrast and waits through the build, then swells to hero size, with 90% of the growth landing exactly on the beat drop.
techniques.use_when: A hero word or product name that should detonate on the drop after a quiet intro. The one appearance of the final wordmark when the music builds into the end. A single-word answer after a question beat.
techniques.avoid_when: There is no real musical hit to land on. Words wide enough to swell past the safe area. Using it more than once per film. Stacking a separate scale punch or camera kick on the same hit.

techniques.name: Centre-out line unmask
techniques.summary: A short line opens from its own centre outward behind a soft-edged mask while the letters stay perfectly still, so a result or status reads as unveiled rather than flown in.
techniques.use_when: A result, status or confirmation line under a centred icon ('Published', 'Connected'). A hero word inside a pill that has just formed. A calm sub-line under a headline that has already landed.
techniques.avoid_when: Lines over about 40 characters (the edges take too long to reach the ends). Left-aligned layouts (wipe from the left edge instead). Text that is also moving, where the mask fights the glyph motion. Headlines that need energy.

techniques.name: Animated line re-break
techniques.summary: A centred one-line statement re-breaks into a two-line stack, or back, with every word gliding from its old slot to its new one, so the layout changes without a cut or a jump.
techniques.use_when: An inserted icon or a longer word makes a centred line too wide. A headline must stack to free half the frame for a product shot. Returning a stacked headline to a single line for the payoff.
techniques.avoid_when: Lines over about 7 words. Re-breaks that carry the hero word far from where it was being read (keep it as the still anchor). More than one re-break per statement. Vertical formats, where a stack is already the default layout.

techniques.name: Orbit gather and merge
techniques.summary: Tokens swing into orbit around a node, slow to a lazy spin, then accelerate one by one into a single exit point from which a line shoots out.
techniques.use_when: Several inputs, funds or sources gather before one action (pooling, batching, syncing, sending) and the idea should be told by physics with no words.
techniques.avoid_when: The tokens are UI cards carrying text (unreadable while orbiting), or the story has no single output point.

techniques.name: Path fractures into a fan, then re-converges
techniques.summary: A solid line draws out, breaks into dashes, splits into a fan of curves that end on obstacle pills, and later the curves funnel back into one point that becomes the next diagram.
techniques.use_when: Explaining the friction of an old way (one simple path turning into many obstacles) before the turn to one clean path.
techniques.avoid_when: The viewer needs real product UI on screen; this is diagram language, and a diagram act longer than about 4 s loses the thread.

techniques.name: Stalled state by dimming
techniques.summary: A token stops on its rail, the destination greys out, short status words appear one after another, and the frame goes briefly still so the blockage is felt.
techniques.use_when: The problem beat: money, a message or a task stuck waiting (closed, pending, rejected) just before the product unblocks it.
techniques.avoid_when: The film has no problem act, or the block would sit longer than about 1.5 s; stillness only works as a short contrast to the motion around it.

techniques.name: Clutter pile-up, then strip to one
techniques.summary: Clicks spawn copies of a control until the frame is a messy pile, then elements vanish one per beat and the survivors snap to re-centre until a single tile remains.
techniques.use_when: Showing overload (too many tools, buttons, tabs, notifications) and then focus: the product reduces chaos to the one thing that matters.
techniques.avoid_when: Calm or premium films, or elements whose text must be read; the jumps are deliberately abrupt.

techniques.name: Cards dealt or dropped into a grid
techniques.summary: Cards land in a row or grid one after another, either dealt fast with a small tilt that squares up, or falling from just in front of the camera and shrinking into their slots.
techniques.use_when: Revealing a set of options, results, features or integrations that should read as one set with a clear reading order.
techniques.avoid_when: There is one hero object, or more than about 8 cards (use a row cascade or a scroll).

techniques.name: Container resizes, content reflows
techniques.summary: A card or window changes size because its content or the user changes it, growing as typed text wraps or narrowing as an edge is dragged, while everything inside reflows to the new width.
techniques.use_when: Typing into an input, responsive layouts, resizable panels: any moment where the point is that the UI adapts.
techniques.avoid_when: The size change is a change of role, such as a button becoming a panel (use a container morph), or text must be read during the resize.

techniques.name: Row cascade
techniques.summary: List rows or cards appear one after another from top to bottom, each rising a few pixels as it fades in, so the list reads as data streaming in.
techniques.use_when: Populating any list, inbox, table, feed or a pair of mirrored input and output columns.
techniques.avoid_when: Rows are added one at a time over a longer beat (top insert), or the list arrives by scrolling (flick scroll).

techniques.name: Fanned stack resolves into slots
techniques.summary: A tilted, overlapping stack of cards spreads into an even row, or each card flips to show its face and flies small into a slot of a list grid where its label resolves.
techniques.use_when: Many options, offers, integrations or tools becoming an orderly set: the 'all in one place' or 'compare them all' beat.
techniques.avoid_when: The cards must be read while they move, or there is only one card.

techniques.name: Lens list scroll
techniques.summary: A list scrolls with momentum past an invisible lens line, and each item's size, tint or tilt depends on its distance from that line, like a phone picker, a rolodex cylinder or a smile-shaped arc.
techniques.use_when: Choosing among options, showing many screens as one continuous surface, or a playful list of choices that read one at a time.
techniques.avoid_when: Items must be read while moving fast, or a plain scroll says it more simply.

techniques.name: Toss into a bin with one rebound
techniques.summary: Icons or chips are thrown into a container that rises in to catch them, drop through its mouth and peek back out once before settling.
techniques.use_when: A comic or decisive 'throw the old way away' beat: replacing old tools, clearing clutter, deleting the problem.
techniques.avoid_when: Serious, calm or enterprise tone, or the film has already used its two spring landings.

techniques.name: Push-aside with bound layout
techniques.summary: An incoming panel or card enters from the edge and the neighbouring content moves aside because it is bound to the panel's edge, so one motion moves two elements and nothing overlaps.
techniques.use_when: Introducing a detail panel, a new card or a caption beside existing UI, or a joke where the layout itself does the gag.
techniques.avoid_when: The incoming element should float above (modal, popover), or there is no room to move into.

techniques.name: Outline-led insert and spawn
techniques.summary: A thin accent line or a heavy outline appears first and opens into a new row or a modal, then the stroke decays to a hairline so the content takes over.
techniques.use_when: A click that creates something (a new account, row, record or dialog) that must read from a wide shot, or repeated creation shown as a rhythm.
techniques.avoid_when: The accent already means something else in the film, or the shot is a calm monochrome close-up where a bright stroke would shout.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Use a flat 2 px stroke in the film's single accent with no box-shadow, bloom or blur; express the flash as stroke width (2 to 3 px for 4 f via hitPulse) and an opacity decay from 1 to 0.4 to 0 over 24 f, and frame the modal with a solid 6-10 px accent stroke that thins to 1 px.

techniques.name: Spawn from the anchor point
techniques.summary: Menus, popovers, drop targets and detail cards scale out of the exact point that caused them, such as the cursor tip or a map pin, and collapse back into it.
techniques.use_when: Any UI that opens from a click, or a drag target appearing: menus, popovers, dialogs, drop zones, cards from a map pin.
techniques.avoid_when: The element enters from off-screen or is a full window (rise-in), or the trigger point is out of frame.

techniques.name: Shell first, then contents, then the action
techniques.summary: The empty container is on screen first, its contents arrive left to right, the card unfolds downward in stages, and the primary button fills last as the clear call to act.
techniques.use_when: The first appearance of any real product screen, especially dashboards, headers and forms whose reading order matters.
techniques.avoid_when: The screen should feel already alive on the cut (enter it moving with a rise-in), or the shot is shorter than about 40 f.

techniques.name: Top insert pushes the list down
techniques.summary: New items arrive at the top of a list one at a time and every earlier item slides down one slot, on a steady metronome that reads as abundance or on a slower cadence where each row resolves as it is generated.
techniques.use_when: Results, messages, subtasks or saved items accumulating: generated rows, imports landing, a feed or a stack filling up.
techniques.avoid_when: The whole list should appear at once (row cascade), or there are so many inserts that the pushes blur into noise (scroll instead).

techniques.name: Container morph into its next role
techniques.summary: One element changes shape into what it becomes, a button unfolding into a panel, a card stretching into a detail view, a pill collapsing into an app tile, so there is no navigation cut to explain.
techniques.use_when: A click that opens something (button to panel, card to detail), a status becoming an icon, an object docking into its slot.
techniques.avoid_when: The size change comes from content or a drag (live reflow), or the two states have no visual relation.

techniques.name: Drag to reorder, siblings make way
techniques.summary: An item lifts under the cursor, travels on a slight arc to a new position while its neighbours slide aside one slot at a time, and settles into place with a firm landing and no bounce.
techniques.use_when: Prioritising, scheduling, kanban boards, playlists: any product whose smart part is ordering things.
techniques.avoid_when: The reorder is automatic (animate the computed reorder on one curve, with no cursor), or more than 2-3 drags would fall in one shot.

techniques.name: Progress spine leads the steps
techniques.summary: A thin line grows down the side of a step list with a dot at its head. Each step appears as the head reaches it, works with a spinner and a typed detail line, then flips to done, and the list scrolls to keep the head in view until the line turns a rounded corner toward the result.
techniques.use_when: An agent, build, deploy, import or onboarding process working through steps, where the point is visible progress toward one result.
techniques.avoid_when: There are fewer than 3 steps (one status capsule says it), or the steps finish too fast to read (show the result with a count instead).
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Draw the head as a flat 10 px dot in C.ink (white on an ink stage) with no halo, bloom or blur. Mark its state with size instead (12 px while travelling, 10 px while waiting). The spine, the step states, the scroll follow and every timing stay the same.

techniques.name: Genie launch from an icon
techniques.summary: A dock or home-screen icon flares open at its top into a curved funnel that keeps widening until it fills the frame, and the app's first screen is already sitting inside it.
techniques.use_when: Opening an app, a document or a tool from its icon in a dock, launcher or home screen, as a playful product-native scene change.
techniques.avoid_when: The product is never launched from an icon, or the film already has a genie (once is a gag, twice reads as a template).
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Fill the funnel with the app's real first screen on its flat stage colour, or with one flat colour taken from the icon, never the icon's colour ramp. The clip path, the log-space growth and the timing stay the same.

techniques.name: Ease-out count-up from a near-final value
techniques.summary: A proof figure counts up in place from a credible value just below its target and decelerates, so the last units tick in one at a time and it reads in about half a second.
techniques.use_when: A single proof figure (countries, users, a price) must register in under a second, or a number inside a UI shot should feel live.
techniques.avoid_when: The number is the film's hero reveal and deserves a reel or a snap-out; nothing on screen causes the count to start.

techniques.name: Companion glyph swaps mid-count
techniques.summary: A small icon riding a counting number (a flag, an avatar, a status glyph) swaps to its destination state when the count crosses a threshold, then drops from superscript to the baseline.
techniques.use_when: The count carries a from-to story (origin to destination, free to paid, pending to done) that one icon can tell.
techniques.avoid_when: The glyph would only be decoration; counts shorter than 20 f, where the swap gets lost.

techniques.name: Process-status pill with ring progress
techniques.summary: A compact capsule shows where a process stands in one glance: a live dot, a mono step label, a ring filled to the current percentage, the step count and a grey date.
techniques.use_when: Proving that a real, structured process exists (pipeline, build, delivery) as an overlay on process footage.
techniques.avoid_when: The step and percentage aren't true to the story; frames that already carry a headline, which the pill would compete with.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: The same capsule on a solid C.ink2 fill with a 1.5 px hairline border, no backdrop blur or frosted translucency, depth only from a soft drop shadow at about 0.16 alpha. Keep the live dot, the ring and the one step line ('Step 5/6 · Motion'); drop the tracked mono uppercase label and the grey date, which only decorate.

techniques.name: Metric as the first statement
techniques.summary: The film opens on its proof number already moving, with no title and no logo, and the brand waits for the end lockup.
techniques.use_when: The product has one strong, true outcome number (users, views, savings) that should earn attention before the name does.
techniques.avoid_when: The number is weak, generic or can't be verified; films where the mark itself must lead.

techniques.name: Tucked unit under the last digits
techniques.summary: A small lowercase unit word fades in right-aligned under a big number's last digits, its top overlapping the numeral's baseline, so number and unit read as one mark.
techniques.use_when: A hero figure needs its unit (views, users, ms) without a second line pushing the layout down.
techniques.avoid_when: The unit is longer than one short word; numbers ending in narrow digits (1, 7) that leave no room to tuck under.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Same placement and size in the film's one sans at weight 450, in C.mute or the stage's secondary ink: no second display typeface and no cream or gold tint.

techniques.name: Hero bar in close-up, then pull back
techniques.summary: The winning bar (or the hero chart) grows across a tight frame, then the camera eases back to show the whole chart, with the grey comparison bars and their values.
techniques.use_when: Benchmarks and comparisons the product wins; any chart whose hero value should be felt before it is compared.
techniques.avoid_when: Narrow wins, which the close-up would oversell; more than ~6 bars, whose labels go unreadable after the pull-back.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: A flat accent bar with no outer glow or bloom. It stands apart from the grey bars by colour and 4-6 px of extra thickness only.

techniques.name: Mini bar-chart answer card
techniques.summary: Inside a chat or a panel, an answer arrives as a small card of labelled horizontal bars that grow in sequence, followed by a one-line insight that states the key figures.
techniques.use_when: An AI or analytics product answers a question with data; a walkthrough needs one piece of quantitative proof.
techniques.avoid_when: More than 6 rows, where the group outruns 30 f and the labels shrink; bars that carry no real meaning.

techniques.name: Line chart draws with a tracking head
techniques.summary: A line or stepped series draws left to right behind a solid dot at its head that the eye can follow, accelerating through the middle and creeping into its last point.
techniques.use_when: Growth, price or usage over time; any chart where the trend is the message.
techniques.avoid_when: Invented up-and-to-the-right data; charts under ~400 px wide, where the head reads as noise.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: A solid head dot with a 2 px stage-colour ring and no blur, drop-shadow halo or bloom. The area fill stays a single-hue opacity ramp.

techniques.name: Constant-speed bar sweep with lit caps
techniques.summary: A row of bars grows in a wave that travels at constant speed; each bar eases up on its own and flashes a bright cap that relaxes to the resting tone.
techniques.use_when: Volume, activity or histogram data streaming in; an opening equaliser or skyline that hints at growth.
techniques.avoid_when: Bars that must be compared precisely, since the wave delays reading; fewer than 6 bars.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Solid single-tone bars (or a single-hue tonal ramp) whose cap uses the film's one accent and relaxes to the bar tone: never a multi-hue gradient and never a warm amber cap.

techniques.name: One control drives several live numbers
techniques.summary: Dragging a slider visibly drives every dependent figure in lockstep, and the fill changes tint once it passes a marked threshold.
techniques.use_when: Calculators, pricing, risk limits, utilisation: any feature whose logic is 'move this and those follow'.
techniques.avoid_when: The dependent figures aren't computed consistently from one formula; more than 3 dependents.

techniques.name: Flag cascade, then one chosen
techniques.summary: Status marks appear on a set of cards one after another, then a single card switches to the accent state: many flagged, one picked.
techniques.use_when: Triage, review, matching, anomaly detection: anything that narrows many down to one.
techniques.avoid_when: The pick isn't what the product actually outputs; grids of more than ~12 cards, where the cascade reads as a queue.

techniques.name: Top-to-bottom row refresh
techniques.summary: When a filter changes, a thin scan line crosses each table row in turn from top to bottom, and the row's icon, label and values change behind it.
techniques.use_when: Tables, activity feeds or leaderboards that refresh on a filter or a new period.
techniques.avoid_when: Only one cell changes, so a Roll on it is enough; more than 8 rows, where the cascade reads as a queue.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: One neutral hairline per row (the accent only on the row the story cares about), with no rainbow-tinted streak and no glow.

techniques.name: Mechanical digit reel
techniques.summary: Each digit sits in its own masked column and rolls vertically like an odometer: the low columns spin while the high ones step once, landing column by column.
techniques.use_when: Counters with a tactile, product-like feel: totals, balances, counters that step on visible events.
techniques.avoid_when: The film already counts with plain in-place digits (keep one counting style per film); fewer than 3 changes, where one roll is enough.

techniques.name: Ring gauge filling with its centre number
techniques.summary: A circular gauge sweeps to its value while the number at its centre counts on the same progress, and the ring's end cap leads the eye around.
techniques.use_when: Percentages, scores, completion and utilisation; status pills and KPI tiles.
techniques.avoid_when: Values that aren't parts of a whole; more than 3 concentric rings.

techniques.name: Before-to-after with a delta chip
techniques.summary: The old figure steps back to a small grey 'before', the new figure counts in at hero size, and a delta chip ('-38%') pops in the accent on the landing frame.
techniques.use_when: Improvements such as cost down, speed up or errors falling from 412 to 3; before-and-after claims.
techniques.avoid_when: The change is small or noisy; the story has no real 'before' state to show.

techniques.name: Unit grid that fills to the count
techniques.summary: A grid of small squares, each standing for a fixed number of units, fills in a diagonal wave while a counter beside it reaches the total, and one cell lands in the accent.
techniques.use_when: Shares and proportions ('3 in 10 teams'), quotas, capacity; making a large count tangible without a chart.
techniques.avoid_when: Exact values with many significant digits, which the grid can't show honestly; cells under 12 px on vertical phone formats.

techniques.name: Area-true ratio comparison
techniques.summary: A multiplier claim ('10x smaller') plays as a block that shrinks in log space to the area the ratio implies, leaving an outline of its old size behind.
techniques.use_when: Multiplier and reduction claims about size, cost, time or footprint.
techniques.avoid_when: Ratios above ~25x, where the block shrinks to a dot (show the number alone); claims that aren't really proportional.

techniques.name: Device rises already moving
techniques.summary: A phone or app window enters from below already travelling on the cut frame and decelerates into place near centre while the whole shot slowly scales down.
techniques.use_when: The first product shot after a type card or a photo, when the previous shot's energy should carry straight into the product.
techniques.avoid_when: The device is already on screen; a calm film where a 20 px/f arrival feels pushy; it would be the third rise in a row (vary with a tilt or a pull-back).

techniques.name: Tilted product plane flattens
techniques.summary: A real product page lies tipped back in perspective, rises toward the camera and rotates flat to face the viewer, landing the product as a frontal screen.
techniques.use_when: Introducing a real web page or app screen as the real thing while keeping the camera alive; the first frontal look at the product.
techniques.avoid_when: The UI must be read during the move; the plane would need more than about 30° of tilt (text shears and aliases); the same flatten ran within the last 10 s.

techniques.name: Hard swap on the cause frame
techniques.summary: On a click or selection the product image, view or value changes in one frame with no crossfade, any price or count rolls up from just below its new value, and a physical card can hide the swap in a small 3D kick.
techniques.use_when: A choice changes the product instantly: a variant picker, filter, plan selector, theme switch, a canvas that appears whole on launch.
techniques.avoid_when: The change is a process the viewer should watch; two numbers would sit half-and-half in place; swaps faster than one per 30 f (the clicks read as a macro).

techniques.name: Generated view resolves from soft
techniques.summary: A freshly generated window or row appears as a soft, out-of-focus shape over a flat placeholder plate and snaps into crisp UI in about a third of a second.
techniques.use_when: An AI or build step produces a result and it should read as just arrived, without a spinner.
techniques.avoid_when: The UI was already on screen (use a state change); more than two resolves in one sequence (it becomes a fog filter); type so small that 12 f of softness hurts legibility.

techniques.name: Agent status beat, then streamed answer
techniques.summary: The product's tiny working status is shown at hero size, as a black capsule with a spinner and a typed label or as bare headline type, holds for a beat with a looping ellipsis or shimmer, then dissolves as the answer streams in.
techniques.use_when: An AI or agent product needs its invisible work made visible, and a moment of anticipation before the payoff.
techniques.avoid_when: The product is not autonomous; the hold would run past about 74 f; a second status beat in the same film.
techniques.ban_safe_variant: Keep the same beat but build every decoration from one hue: a flat C.ink capsule with a plain soft neutral drop shadow instead of coloured light blobs behind it, a dot spinner or clock glyph instead of a sparkle icon, a shimmer made of three lightness stops of one grey instead of a multi-hue sweep, and an accent-to-ink trail on the newest characters instead of a multi-colour wake.

techniques.name: Headline becomes the product input
techniques.summary: Without a cut the headline turns into the product: a caret appears in the gap between two words, swells into a capsule and widens into the input bar that shoves the words aside, or the sentence inside a card dissolves while the card reshapes into the input.
techniques.use_when: Bridging from message to demo in a type-led film; the product's core surface is an input, search or command bar.
techniques.avoid_when: The product is not input-led; the headline has no natural gap; the bar would have to stay translucent over a busy backdrop (go straight to opaque).

techniques.name: Fast prompt at true scale
techniques.summary: The real prompt bar fills with a long, honest instruction in about a second at full legible size, the card growing as lines wrap, then the text is sent up into a chat bubble.
techniques.use_when: An AI, search or command product whose real input is the story; showing a real task without a dull typing wait.
techniques.avoid_when: The prompt runs past about 100 characters (cut it); a human-paced beat is the point (use 30 cps with human rhythm); the product is not input-driven.

techniques.name: Mark docks into the app
techniques.summary: An integration mark or icon travels to an app tile or page and settles overlapping its face, rising in front of it at the moment of contact, so it reads as plugging in.
techniques.use_when: An integration, plug-in or works-inside claim; handing off from a settings screen into the platform it acts on.
techniques.avoid_when: The mark would pass over text being read; the mark is also the end lockup (it would appear early, so dock an integration icon instead).

techniques.name: Edit with the product's own UI
techniques.summary: Instead of cuts, the film moves between product areas the way the app does: a window recedes to a corner, a sheet slides up, a popover pops from its anchor, a button or card unfolds into a full panel.
techniques.use_when: Walkthroughs across several product areas; any film where each transition can also demonstrate how the product navigates.
techniques.avoid_when: A purely conceptual or type-led film; desktop chrome that is not part of the brand world; more than one native transition every 3 s (it starts to feel like a screen recording).

techniques.name: Shared element survives the page change
techniques.summary: The cursor clicks a row; the page drains away except the row's icon (or the clicked card), which stays exactly in place while the next page assembles around it with a short zoom-out.
techniques.use_when: Navigating into a detail view, or carrying a piece of content between apps, where spatial continuity should make the product feel instant.
techniques.avoid_when: Nothing exists in both states; the anchor is under about 40 px and cannot carry attention; it would need to travel more than a third of the frame (use a native transition).

techniques.name: Flick scroll lands the target
techniques.summary: A list or page scrolls like a trackpad flick, entering already fast or ramping up briefly, then glides on an exponential tail until the target row rests at its reading position.
techniques.use_when: Showing volume (many results, a long page, a feed), or moving down a form to its next section with a human feel.
techniques.avoid_when: The viewer must read during the move; the list is shorter than two screens; it would be the third scroll in a row.

techniques.name: One native control as the demo
techniques.summary: Instead of a screenshot, the feature is shown as the single control that embodies it (a picker wheel, a toggle, a segmented switch) at large scale, centred, with no chrome, doing only its native interaction.
techniques.use_when: A settings, targeting or compatibility claim in a type-led film, where one interaction says it is a real product faster than a full UI.
techniques.avoid_when: The feature needs context to make sense; the control is generic (every app has a toggle) and says nothing about the claim.

techniques.name: Drag assets in, skeletons fill
techniques.summary: The cursor drags a fanned stack of images into the input; after the drop they appear as grey skeleton thumbnails that fill with the real images one by one.
techniques.use_when: The product takes real material as input (files, photos, documents) and the viewer should see that context going in.
techniques.avoid_when: The input is text only; the drag path would cross text being read; more than six assets (show a count chip instead).

techniques.name: Pin field pull-back
techniques.summary: A map pulls back from a close view to reveal a field of location pins that drop in as accent marks and relax to ink, then a card grows out of the pin the cursor picks.
techniques.use_when: Location, coverage, store-finder or delivery features; any everywhere claim backed by real places.
techniques.avoid_when: Fewer than about five locations; a map style busy enough to hide the pins; a route arc has already run on the same map.

techniques.name: Before/after drag divider
techniques.summary: The cursor grabs a vertical divider on the product and drags it across, wiping away the old state to reveal the new one in the same layout.
techniques.use_when: Redesigns, image or audio cleanup, performance gains, any this-got-better claim with a visible difference.
techniques.avoid_when: The two states differ in layout (the wipe then reads as a glitch); the difference is invisible at frame size; the film has no human gesture anywhere else.

techniques.name: Long page flown like a runway
techniques.summary: A whole long page lies on a steeply tilted plane that recedes to a horizon, and the view travels along it faster and faster, so the page reads as one landscape and is cut at full speed.
techniques.use_when: Showing the length or completeness of a page, document, feed or site in about a second without asking anyone to read it; a fast connective beat between two readable product shots, or the carrier for a change made mid-move, such as a theme switch.
techniques.avoid_when: The content must be read, the page is short (it reads as a tilted card instead), or the frame is vertical and leaves too little runway; use it once per film.

techniques.name: Ghost suggestion accepted with a key
techniques.summary: As someone types, the product proposes the rest of the line as pale ghost text after the caret; a small key chip appears, the key is pressed, and the ghost text inks in left to right as the caret jumps to its end.
techniques.use_when: An assistant that completes text, code, email or form fields inline: the moment the product does the work is one key away, and the cause (the key) and the effect (the ink) share a frame.
techniques.avoid_when: The product generates whole answers rather than inline completions (stream the answer instead), or the suggestion runs past about two lines at readable size; never show more than two accepts in a row.

techniques.name: List narrows with each keystroke
techniques.summary: A shortcut opens a command palette or search field, and as the query types the list answers every key: non-matching rows fold away, survivors slide up, matched letters ink in, and the highlight rides the top result until Enter.
techniques.use_when: Search, command menus, filters and pickers: any product whose speed claim is 'type a few letters and it is there', proving instant results without a spinner.
techniques.avoid_when: The rows are illegible at frame size (punch in first), or the query is long (past about 12 characters it becomes a typing beat); do not FLIP more than about ten rows at once.

techniques.name: Scrub a chart with a live readout
techniques.summary: The cursor glides across a chart; a hairline and a dot ride the series beneath it and a small readout shows the date and value at that point, stepping from data point to data point until it lands on the one that makes the claim.
techniques.use_when: Analytics, finance, health or monitoring products whose value is reading any point in history; a calm interaction beat after a fast one.
techniques.avoid_when: The chart has no point worth landing on, or the readout is illegible at the framing (punch in to 1.6-2x first); never scrub faster than the readout can be read.

techniques.name: Command runs, output prints in bursts
techniques.summary: A command is typed at human speed and entered; the terminal answers machine-fast, printing whole lines in uneven bursts with a stepping spinner and a progress bar, and ends on a single success line.
techniques.use_when: Developer tools, CLIs, infrastructure and build products, where the contrast between a human-typed command and machine-fast output is the speed claim.
techniques.avoid_when: The audience is not technical, or the output itself must be read line by line (show the result screen instead); never type the output.

techniques.name: Change applied as a visible diff
techniques.summary: A proposed edit lands in a code or document view as a diff: outgoing lines strike through and fold away, incoming lines open in place with a marker in the gutter, and the view steps hunk by hunk before the change is accepted.
techniques.use_when: AI coding or writing assistants and review, versioning or migration tools, when the claim is 'it changes exactly the right lines and shows you which'.
techniques.avoid_when: The code is unreadable at frame size (macro in first), or the change needs more than three hunks (show a summary instead); never give removals a second colour.

techniques.name: Several people at work at once
